207.text:
ADR 0018: The API review for 5.0.0

Status: Accepted
Date: 2026-11-01

Context
Release 5.0.0 should be the last that breaks an API or a self-hoster for a long time, so a break is
accepted now wherever it removes a later one. This ADR reviews packages/contracts/openapi.json,
the snapshot and feed, problem codes, auth, and what a self-hoster depends on.
What 4.0.0 shipped, checked in the tag: no /api/v1, no OpenAPI document and no API docs. It had
the ad hoc routes /api/admin/* (seeding), /api/toggle-rsvp, /api/add-session and the like,
/api/auth/login and /api/health. The 5.0.0 steps already deleted all of them except
/api/health and POST /api/auth/logout (point 4). So /api/v1 has never been released: any
change to it breaks nobody, and the one break that does reach users (the 4.0.0 routes are gone) is
named in the CHANGELOG.md breaking note.
Decision
The path

/api/v1 stays. It is unreleased, so the name costs nothing, and the policy below says what
a v2 would take. /api/health stays beside /api/v1/health as the probe for monitors and the
Docker healthcheck; it is not versioned and never changes meaning.

Endpoints
Benefit and who breaks are given for each change. Since /api/v1 is unreleased, “breaks” means
“changes what the SPA calls” unless stated.

Remove GET /guests/{id}/rsvps. Nothing calls it; the snapshot’s me.rsvps and
GET /sessions/{id}/rsvps answer the same questions. Benefit: one promise fewer. Breaks nobody.
Remove DELETE /me/identity. POST /auth/sign-out does the same and also ends a verified
session. Benefit: one way to end a login session. Breaks nobody (the SPA moves to
/auth/sign-out).
POST /api/auth/logout becomes DELETE /api/v1/auth/site. It is a third sign-out path,
outside the versioned API and unlisted in the document; the SPA uses it to end the site-password
login and the login session together. As a method on the site-login resource it is documented
beside POST /auth/site. Breaks nobody (unreleased; only the SPA calls it).
Keep GET /updates, GET /attendees, GET /host-clashes and GET /sessions/{id}/rsvps.
The candidate list said nothing uses them; the SPA does (footer, people directory, session form,
admin RSVP list). They answer what the replica cannot: the release status, the site-wide
directory, a private-aware clash check, and who RSVPed. /attendees (every guest of the site)
and /guests (one event’s guests) keep their names; the docs say how they differ.
Methods, not verbs, for removing one thing. POST /me/notifications/delete becomes
DELETE /me/notifications?ids=…; POST /me/push-subscriptions/remove becomes
DELETE /me/push-subscriptions?endpoint=…; POST /me/push-subscriptions/check becomes
GET /me/push-subscriptions?endpoint=… (it changes nothing). Benefit: HTTP methods say what
happens, so proxies, clients and the retry rules treat them right. Breaks nobody. The push
endpoint now appears in proxy access logs; accepted, since it is useless without the keys, and
the SPA sends no idempotency key with that DELETE (it is idempotent), so the server does not
store the endpoint either. Ids in the URL are capped at 100 per call.
Keep the command pairs …/guests/assign|remove and …/locations/assign|remove under an
event. They set membership from a list in one transaction; remove as DELETE would need a
body. The rule written into api.md: a POST with a verb is a command that is not a plain
create, update or removal of one resource (accept, decline, cancel, move, assign,
remove, read); a removal of one resource is DELETE.
/admin/… is a promise about privilege, not about the role. /admin/sessions and
/admin/proposals differ from /sessions and /proposals in what they do (any phase, on behalf
of hosts, adminManaged), not only in who may call them, so they stay. Today they need a site
admin; a later organizer role may be allowed on the per-event ones. Widening who may call an
endpoint is not a break; narrowing is. The role is checked in the use case and shows in the
endpoint’s description, never in a path, so the organizer role fits without a change.
Events: {id} for resources, {slug} for the schedule. Both are immutable after creation
(an event update cannot change the slug), so both are stable keys. The snapshot and feed use the
slug because it is the address people see; everything else uses the id. Documented, not changed.
POST /dev/reminders leaves the API. It moves to /api/dev/reminders, outside /api/v1
and outside openapi.json, still answering 404 unless SB_ENABLE_DEV_TOOLS is set. Benefit:
the public document promises only what operators and scripts may use. Breaks nobody.

Auth

SITE_PASSWORD and POST /auth/site stay for all of 5.x. The read setting (ADR 0017
point 11) later makes the gate unnecessary: then SITE_PASSWORD logs a deprecation warning and
keeps working, and /auth/site keeps answering, until a major release removes them.
API tokens use Authorization: Bearer sb_…, resolved by the actor middleware into the same
actor as a cookie with the token’s scopes; cookie-only checks (Origi

220.title: ADR 0019: Statistics in the admin
220.text:
ADR 0019: Statistics in the admin

Status: Accepted
Date: 2026-11-07
Issue: #389

Context
Organizers want to know, during and after an event, whether the process worked (proposals, votes,
sessions, attendance), whether the venue worked and which features people used (issue #389). The
data is in the database, but an admin sees only counts today, and the one number that measures
success, the attendee count, is kept out of every admin surface by
ADR 0007 §3. The figures and their data are listed
in Statistics: figures. No real event database is available to the project
(privacy), so old data is checked through the release-upgrade fixtures and the dev seed.
Decision
Principles

No new disclosure. The page shows a site admin nothing the admin cannot see elsewhere, except
as aggregates. Today an admin sees vote counts per proposal, never who voted what. That stays
true. One exception: the reported attendee count per session. This ADR supersedes the part of ADR
0007 §3 that keeps it out of the admin read surface and of exports (see below).
Names only where already public: titles, hosts, locations. People who only voted, RSVPed or
requested a 1-on-1 never appear by name.
Per-person tables are not joinable. A per-person table (e.g. “votes per voter”) has no guest
id, a pseudonym (P001…) assigned per table and per request in sorted order, and rows sorted by
value. Two tables can therefore not be joined to rebuild a person. Relations across domains (“do
voters RSVP more?”) are computed on the server and shown as aggregates.
Small numbers are suppressed in free text. Values of free-text fields (based in, meeting
point, languages) appear only when at least 3 people share them; the rest is “Other”.
Honest correlations. A correlation shows Spearman’s ρ with n, and below n = 15 the text
“too few to say”. A trend line is drawn only from n = 15 and does not imply cause. (See the
attendance model: 13 sessions gave p ≈ 0.07.)

Read-only, on the server
No new disclosure beyond the above, and no storage: statistics are computed on read from the current
tables: no new table, no migration, no change-log entry. A read-only module server/modules/stats
has one use case, eventStatistics(actor, eventId, filter), for site admins only. A
StatsRepository read port loads the event’s raw facts in a few bulk queries and the figures are
computed in TypeScript, in pure functions in packages/domain/src/stats/ (interval math, rank
correlation, binning, pseudonyms, suppression, CSV encoding, the attendance prediction). An event is
small, so this is fast and testable. The prediction of the
attendance model is shown next to the reported count, labelled with
its basis (one event, n = 13).
The filter
One past event: rooms “Volunteers N”, every session there hosted by one organizer account. Manual
removal in a CSV does not work for the figures that matter most: unique hosts, room utilization,
parallel sessions, RSVPs per attendee. So the filter applies on the server, to every table, chart
and CSV.
Generic facets, no event-specific concept:

Exclude locations (checkbox list). A session with all its locations excluded is excluded; the
location disappears from location tables.
Exclude hosts (checkbox list of hosts). A session whose hosts are all excluded is excluded.
The host also leaves every people figure (members, voters, RSVPs, 1-on-1s, profiles): an organizer
account is not an attendee.
Exclude origins: blocker (default excluded), organizer, spontaneous, proposal.

The filter lives in the URL query only (nothing stored), so a filtered view is a link and the CSV
link carries it. The page shows the active filter in one line (“Excluding 4 locations, 1 host,
blockers”); the CSV file name carries a short form (my-event-sessions-filtered.csv).
Every session table keeps locations, hosts and origin columns, so a CSV user can filter
further by hand.
Later, when session kinds (not-built.md: session, shift, fixture) exist, shifts and fixtures are
excluded by default and the facets stay for the rest.
An excluded session still occupies its room, so location gaps stay true.
Session origin
Derived, a heuristic, stated on the page: blocker when blocker is set; else proposal when
proposal_id is set; else organizer when admin_managed; else spontaneous. A deleted proposal
turns its session into “spontaneous” (proposal_id is set null); an admin can untick admin-managed.
The table contract

Contract: a generic StatsTable (id, title, columns: {key, label, type}[], rows),
with column types text | integer | number | percent | minutes | datetime | boolean. One table
component renders all of them; charts are bound by table id. A datetime cell is a string the
server already formatted in the event’s zone (YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm, as in the CSV), so the payload
needs no zone and the table shows it as given.
API: GET /api/v1/admin/events/{id}/stats?{filter} (JSON, all tables) and
GET /api/v1/admin/events/{id}/stats/{table}.csv?{filter}. The server writes the CSV, so one
encoder serves

244.title: Decisions
244.text:
Decisions
The decisions behind the shape, each with the alternatives that lost. The numbered ADRs in
…/adr/ record the individual steps; these are the ones that hold the whole
design together.

D1 · API server plus static SPA, no server-side rendering
Context. The app was Next.js with server components and server actions as the data path. Live
updates, an OpenAPI document, bots and a clear frontend/backend line all need a real HTTP API, so
the question was whether to keep server-side rendering (SSR) next to it.
Decision. One process serves an OpenAPI-described HTTP API, an SSE change feed and a static
React SPA built with Vite. The first HTML is a static shell. React stays.
Why not SSR. Its gains are small here: the app is behind a login (no search engines), and an
installed PWA opens from disk with no round trip, which SSR cannot beat and which works offline. Its
costs are real: two runtimes for one UI, hydration bugs (“which code ran where”), server-rendered
truth that live updates overwrite on load, and no offline path without the client render path
anyway.
Alternatives. A meta-framework rendering from the API keeps the hydration cost and still needs
the client store. Next full-stack with a side API gives two data paths.
Consequences. An API contract, a generated client and a client store to maintain. The cold first
load downloads the bundle.

D2 · Guests with assurance levels; picking a name stays viable
Context. Attendees valued having nothing to remember, but private features mean nothing if
anyone can pick a name, and some events will want everyone verified.
Decision. Each login session has an assurance level, claimed or verified. An event’s
identity mode sets the minimum and a guest can raise theirs by protecting their name. Verification
is passwordless first (personal join link, emailed code) with a password as one more option. Roles
are data: the site-admin role on a guest. There is no shared admin password; the site password still
gates the whole site until the read setting replaces it (not-built.md).
Alternatives. Verified only (friction for events with no emails). Protection as the only
mechanism (no way for an organizer to require it).
Consequences. Organizers distribute join links. ADR 0017.

D3 · A per-event replica kept current by a change feed
Context. The schedule must update without reloads, the views cut across sessions, RSVPs and
meetings, and venue wifi drops.
Decision. The client loads a snapshot of everything its viewer may see of one event and applies
changes from an SSE feed by sequence number; the replica is persisted for offline opening. Paged or
role-restricted data uses ordinary queries.
Alternatives. A query cache with invalidation (every cross-cutting view needs an endpoint or
client joins; offline is partial). A sync engine such as Replicache or Electric (a heavy dependency,
usually Postgres).
Consequences. Purpose-built sync code (feed-apply.ts, the feed client, persistence), a
visibility model that decides the audience at write time, and payloads that carry the full subject.
ADR 0014.

D4 · A Meeting is its own aggregate
Decision. A 1-on-1 Meeting has its own lifecycle (request, accept, decline, cancel) and
two-party privacy, separate from Session; the client merges both where a screen needs them.
Alternative. One calendar-item type including meetings: privacy and lifecycle become optional
fields everywhere.

D5 · Workspace packages as the boundary mechanism
Decision. domain, contracts, api-client and apps/web are Bun workspace packages with
TypeScript project references; dependency-cruiser and ESLint rules guard the boundaries inside
server/ and apps/web. The server stays at the repository root (no apps/server).
Alternative. Directories in one package with lint rules only: less tooling, every boundary
exemptable. ADR 0010.

D6 · SQLite only, behind ports
Decision. SQLite in WAL mode is the only supported database. Repositories are ports, so another
adapter is possible; it is not promised, and several replicas are a non-goal.
Alternatives. Both databases (double the persistence maintenance); Postgres only (a second
container for self-hosters, harder backups).

D7 · Server-Sent Events, not WebSockets
Decision. The feed is SSE with resume by sequence number; mutations go over HTTP.
Why. The client never pushes over the socket; SSE reconnects itself, passes ordinary proxies and
needs no library.

D8 · The change log as the single backbone
Decision. Every use case records changes in the same transaction as its state. The log serves
the feed, notifications and the reactions the jobs loop runs.
Alternatives. Event sourcing (a large mental-model cost for no need here); one mechanism per
concern (an email outbox, a notification table, a pub/sub for the UI).
Consequences. Payload shapes are part of the contract, retention is a limit, and reactions must
be idempotent. ADR 0011.

D9 · Vite, TanStack Router, a small reactive store
Decision. Vite builds the SPA; TanStack Router gives

259.title: Glossary
259.text:
Glossary
The words used in the code and the docs. A word that already means something to attendees keeps that
meaning.



Term
Meaning




Site
One installation, with site settings, guests and events.


Event
One conference or weekend, with days, locations, phases and members. “Something that happened in the system” is a change, not an event.


Day
A calendar date of an event in the event’s time zone, with a booking window.


Phase
Proposal, voting or scheduling. Derived from the event’s phase dates and the clock, never stored.


Location
A room or area where a session happens, with an optional image, colour and unavailable times. A meeting point is where a 1-on-1 happens.


Guest
A person known to the site: name, profile, optional email, password and username. Site-wide.


Member
A guest assigned to an event.


Proposal
An idea for a session, with hosts, votes and comments.


Vote
Interested, maybe or skip, one per guest per proposal. A host sees the breakdown.


Session
Something on the schedule: title, hosts, locations, start and end, capacity.


RSVP
A guest’s commitment to attend a session. Counts toward capacity.


Meeting
A 1-on-1 between two guests in a slot, at a meeting point, with a request, accept, decline or cancel lifecycle.


Actor (internal)
Who acts in a request: a guest with an assurance level, a site admin, or the system.


Assurance
How sure the server is that the actor is the guest: claimed (picked a name) or verified (password, emailed code, join link).


Identity mode
An event’s setting, open or verified, for the assurance its actions need.


Login session
A server-side row for one browser’s sign-in, referenced by the cookie.


Join link
A personal link that signs a guest in and adds them to an event.


Change
A recorded fact: type, subject, actor, time, payload, audience. Committed with the state it describes.


Change log
The append-only changes table, ordered by seq.


Change feed
The per-viewer SSE stream of changes the viewer’s audience permits, resumable from a seq.


Audience
Who may see a change, stored with it.


Snapshot
Everything one viewer may see of one event, at one seq.


Replica
The client’s copy of a snapshot, kept current by the feed and persisted for offline use.


Reaction (internal)
A jobs-loop handler that turns recorded changes into notifications, at least once.


Delivery
One email or push for one guest, sent by the jobs loop with retries.


Use case (internal)
One command or query in a module’s application/: authorize, load, apply the rules, record changes, respond.


Kernel (internal)
The server’s shared code in server/kernel/: unit of work, change log, actor, Result.

261.title: Not built
261.text:
Not built
Designs that were written down and are not in the code, and the questions still open. Nothing here
is committed to until an ADR adopts it. The earlier long form of the design is in the jj history of
docs/dev/target-architecture/.
Designed, not built

Session kinds. Session with a kind of session, shift (a volunteer slot with a minimum
headcount and a “needs people” list) or fixture (an organizer item on everyone’s agenda, such as a
meal), plus latecomer and RSVP-requirement attributes.
Private marks and the personal agenda. A star, hide or note per guest on a session, proposal
or person, visible to nobody else (no query returns another guest’s marks), and an agenda view
that merges what a guest hosts, RSVPed to or starred, with clash groups.
Booking rules. Reserved windows per place and time (organizer only, spontaneous sessions only
from an hour before, a maximum length) and a per-day override of bookable places.
Places. One Place model for rooms, areas, meeting points and “anywhere” (with a gathering
point text), carrying floor, directions and a pin on the venue map. Today locations and meeting
points are separate tables.
Other ways to sign in and be reached. Passkeys, API tokens (hashed, scoped, revocable) for
bots, a QR sheet of join links, chat channels (Telegram, Matrix, Signal) as outbound notification
adapters behind the email and push ones.
Roles. The organizer role on a participation, with per-event admin rights; today only the
site-admin role exists.
The read setting (ADR 0017 point 11): an event readable
by public, by link (a secret event link, rotatable, hidden from the root list) or by
participants (the default). With it comes a public read-only schedule without a login, a kiosk
device link, and the end of SITE_PASSWORD.
Account export and deletion, with deleted guests’ changes anonymised, and a data collection
statement generated from the schema.
Scheduled jobs table. Reminders run as a loop job over the sessions’ reminder rows; a general
scheduled_jobs table does not exist.
Tooling for agents. Module READMEs in a fixed template, scaffolds (make new-use-case), an
ESLint rule that every use case calls a rule before it saves, and golden snapshots per role that
fail when a field becomes visible to a new role.
Translation. User-visible strings as keys with a catalogue; policies already return reason
codes, but the sentences are written in the SPA.
apps/server. The server stays at the repository root; moving it into apps/ was drawn, not
needed.

Open questions
Numbered, each with a recommendation. When one is decided, put the outcome in the chapter it
affects, or in an ADR.

Rate limit keying. Claimed-name guests share one API bucket per address (burst 1000); at a
venue behind one Wi-Fi address, or with SB_TRUSTED_PROXIES unset, all attendees share it.
Recommendation: key by address plus guest cookie with a cap per address (a guest cookie is not
tied to a login session, so any id buys a fresh bucket).
Comment likes. The SPA has neither the “Liked by” hover preview nor the avatars the old
comments had. Recommendation: add both when comments are next touched; the data is in the
snapshot already.
A session that loses its only room reads moved to No location (was Room A) in notices.
Recommendation: reword to “no longer has a location (was Room A)”.
User menu keyboard support: the roles copy the old markup without arrow keys. Recommendation:
use the ARIA menu pattern when the menu is next changed.
Picking a name without being a member. The SPA picker offers only the snapshot’s guests
(members and hosts), because GET /guests is closed to anonymous visitors, so a non-member
cannot pick their name. Recommendation: a public guest-name list for the picker that exposes
names only.

265.title: Architecture rules
265.text:
Architecture rules
Conventions that only live in a document decay. These are the ones the build checks, and where each
kind belongs.
Two mechanisms, split by what they can see:



Mechanism
Sees
Good for




ESLint
one file at a time
banned calls, banned syntax, required shapes


dependency-cruiser
the whole module graph
cycles, layer boundaries, “X may not reach Y”



Run them with make lint and make arch; make precommit runs both.
ESLint: rules about code inside a file
Most single-file rules need no plugin. no-restricted-syntax takes
esquery selectors, so a rule is one selector plus the sentence
you want the author to read:
{
  selector: "NewExpression[callee.name='Date'][arguments.length=0]",
  message: "`new Date()` reads an ambient clock. …",
}

Scope it with a config block listing the enforced areas in files. The ambient-clock ban (ADR 0004)
is the worked example: it covers db/, emails/, packages/ and utils/.
Exempt a line, not a file, with eslint-disable-next-line <rule> -- <reason>. A file-wide ignores
entry would stop checking the other hundred lines too, and an exemption is usually one call in an
otherwise ordinary file. The -- reason is mandatory: it is what the next reader has instead of
this page.
Gotcha: a files entry that matches nothing looks exactly like one that works. Flat config
globs are minimatch, so [ and ( in a path are glob syntax, not literal characters.
When a selector can’t express the rule, write a local rule inline — flat config takes a plugin
object literally, so there is no package to publish and no build step:
const local = {
  rules: {
    "my-rule": {
      create(context) {
        /* … */
      },
    },
  },
};
export default tseslint.config({
  plugins: { local },
  rules: { "local/my-rule": "error" },
});

Because projectService is on, such rules get the TypeScript type checker, not just the syntax
tree.
dependency-cruiser: rules about the module graph
ESLint reads one file at a time, so it cannot see a cycle or a layer violation three hops out.
.dependency-cruiser.cjs holds those. A rule is a from set, a to set, and the reason:
{
  name: "domain-stays-pure",
  severity: "error",
  comment: "why this edge is wrong, and what to do instead",
  from: { path: "^packages/domain/" },
  to: { pathNot: "^packages/domain/" },
}

dependencyTypesNot: ["type-only"] would narrow a rule to runtime edges only — a useful escape
valve mid-migration, when a shared type is still declared on the wrong side of a boundary. One rule
uses it, by decision: a use case may name the db/ container’s repository types until its ports are
its own (use-cases-take-only-container-types, ADR 0012). Otherwise an import the compiler erases
still points the wrong way, and a boundary that holds only at runtime is one nobody can reason about
from the import list.
The direction that matters is inward. db/ is an adapter and may depend on the workspace packages;
the packages may not depend on it (ADR 0010). packages/domain
imports nothing but itself and luxon, and packages/contracts only domain and zod. Types
follow the same direction: an entity type is domain vocabulary and belongs in domain, where both
adapters can import it. A type that only means something to the database — a row shape, a driver’s
handle — stays in db/ and is used only inside db/.
db/repositories/ holds the repository ports and their SQLite adapters, and nothing outside db/
imports from it (repositories-stay-in-db); the rest of the app reaches the repositories through
@/db/container. A port’s input or page type stays next to the port while only db/ uses it; once
code outside db/ needs to name it, it is vocabulary and moves to domain.
server/ follows ADR 0012: server/kernel/ reaches no module, no HTTP
and no framework, not even through a helper it imports; a module’s application/ imports no HTTP,
framework or db/ code; a module is imported only through its module.ts, by other modules and
tests alike. See The server and the API.
utils/ does not import the repository container (@/db/container) directly: it reads through
pageReads() or a use case. Exempt: the job loop, notification and push infrastructure
(utils/jobs/, utils/notifications.ts, utils/push.ts).
apps/web (ADR 0015) imports packages/domain,
packages/contracts and packages/api-client only: never server/, utils/ or db/. Nothing
imports it, features/ never imports api-client (screens call commands/ and queries/), and it
may import only what its own package.json declares. See The web app.
make arch-graph renders the graph to arch-graph.svg (needs graphviz), which is usually faster
than arguing about where a boundary should go.
Adding a rule

Write it, and check that it fails on a file that violates it — a mis-scoped rule reports
success and enforces nothing.
Fix the violations it finds, or list them as exemptions with the reason. Prefer fixing: an
exemption

270.title: Attendance prediction from voting results
270.text:
Attendance prediction from voting results
Fits a formula predicting session attendance from Schelling Board votes, using the 2025 event (259
attendees, 9 parallel sessions, 13 sessions with reported attendance).



File
What it is




data-2025.csv
The data, machine-readable and anonymised. Source of truth


model.py
Constants, data loading, the fitted formula. Import this


attendance-2025.md
The write-up — publishable as-is. Generated


explore.py
Why this model form: candidate comparison by leave-one-out error


validate.py
Significance, bootstrap CIs, variance decomposition, calibration


make_report.py
Regenerates attendance-2025.md from the CSV



uv run explore.py
uv run validate.py
uv run make_report.py   # after editing the CSV

Sessions are numbered by interest share, highest first. The report is written to be publishable: no
titles, and the commentary is kept quantitative so a session cannot be recognised from its
description.
Result
Midpoint, then a range around it:
M      = 0.66 × (N / P) × (s / s̄)
range  = M / g  …  M × g          g = exp(z · σ)
σ      = sqrt( 0.31 + (1 − s) / (s · V) )

s = Interested ÷ total votes on the session, s̄ = event-wide mean of s, N = attendees, P =
parallel sessions, V = people who voted on that session. z = 0.674 for a 50% range, 1.282 for
80%.
Maybe votes are deliberately excluded — every non-zero weight on them made predictions worse.
Where the number of voters enters
Only in the width, never in the midpoint. s is a share, so doubling turnout at the same
proportions leaves the prediction unchanged; what changes is confidence in it, via the binomial term
(1 − s)/(s · V). At 2025 turnout that term is only ~10% of total error — the 0.31 intrinsic
variance is the floor, and no amount of voting reduces it.
Calibration on 2025: 50% range caught 62% of sessions, 80% range caught 77% (a session counts as
caught if the host’s recalled range overlaps the predicted one at all).
Caveats
With n=13 the vote–attendance correlation is not statistically significant (p ≈ 0.07 on log
attendance, 0.19 on ranks). The exponent on s/s̄ is pinned to 1 rather than fitted: the in-sample
best is 0.66, but that is overfitting — the bootstrap CI spans [-0.17, 1.28] and 1 cross-validates
best.
The turnout term is derived from binomial theory, not measured: every session in 2025 got 99–107
votes, so there is no variation to fit against. It also assumes voters are representative of
attendees, which at 40% turnout is a real assumption — k is silently absorbing any bias there.
RSVPs predict far better (log R² 0.63 vs 0.20) but arrive after hosts have already picked a room,
and once you know them the vote adds nothing on top.

285.title: Changelog and release notes
285.text:
Changelog and release notes
The changelog
Update CHANGELOG.md
under [Unreleased] alongside any user-facing change.
Audience: event organizers, not developers. Plain language, no jargon (framework names,
file/function names, library versions) — describe what changed for them, not how it was implemented.
Sections (Keep a Changelog order; use only what applies):

Added — new features
Changed — changes to existing behavior
Deprecated — features being phased out
Removed — removed features
Fixed — bug fixes
Security — vulnerability fixes
Internal — dev-only changes (tooling, tests, refactors, CI) with no visible effect on organizers

Conventions:

One bullet per change, at most two lines:
- **Bold lead phrase** (#123): what changed, and — where it isn't obvious — what was wrong before
Reference the GitHub issue when one exists, taken from the commit’s fixes #123 / issue #123
footer (not the PR number in a squashed subject)
Several commits delivering one feature get one bullet between them
Order bullets within a section roughly by importance
Breaking changes: > **Breaking change**: ... blockquote at the top of the release
Leave out rationale, implementation, edge cases and how a bug was found — those belong in the
commit message, an ADR or these developer docs
Internal is not a second commit history: only internal changes that are particularly valuable,
disruptive or a highlight, around three per release, one line each

The full rules, with the hard limits and worked examples, are in
AGENTS.md § Changelog.
In-app release notes
The app carries a much shorter version of the changelog:
packages/domain/src/release-notes.ts,
shown when the footer’s version is clicked. It holds 3–5 highlights of the coming release —
inline markdown, taking the same bold lead phrase as the changelog bullets.
Add yours to the first entry — the undated "Unreleased" one — as the change lands, and replace a
weaker highlight rather than adding a sixth. Finalizing the release gives that entry its version and
date, after checking its highlights against the changelog — see
Releasing a new version.

289.title: Coding Guidelines
289.text:
Coding Guidelines
Code style

TypeScript strict mode throughout
Mutations go through a use case in server/modules/ and the /api/v1 API
Tailwind CSS for all styling
All UI must be mobile-responsive

Comments
Comment the WHY, not the WHAT. The code already says what it does; a comment earns its place
only by adding something the reader can’t get from reading it — the constraint, the bug, the
surprising interaction, the alternative that was tried and failed.
Default to no comment. Write one when:

a line looks wrong or arbitrary until you know the reason (a workaround, a browser quirk, an
ordering constraint, a magic number)
a file or exported function has a non-obvious purpose or scope
the logic is genuinely intricate and a one-line summary saves the reader reconstructing it

Do not write:

restatements of the code — // toggle the like, // loop over the sessions,
// set loading to true
doc blocks on self-explanatory functions, or @param/@returns that only repeat the signature.
TypeScript types are the documentation
section banners (// ---- helpers ----), commented-out code, or notes about the change being made
(// now also handles X, // new in v2) — that belongs in the commit message
comments that will silently go stale because they duplicate a value or behavior defined elsewhere

Keep them short: one or two lines is usually enough, and prefer prose over ceremony. Longer is fine
when the reason genuinely needs it (an ADR-sized constraint, a subtle race), but that should be
rare.
// Bad — says what the code says
// Get the guest and check if they are a host
const guest = await getActingGuest();
if (guest?.id === session.hostId) {

// Good — says what the code can't
// Hosts bypass the vote check: they can always edit their own session, even
// after voting closes.

This guideline outranks consistency with surrounding code. If a file is full of noisy comments,
don’t match it — write the sparse version. Removing an obsolete or redundant comment in code you’re
already touching is welcome; a sweeping comment-cleanup pass across untouched files is not.
Colours
Never write a palette shade (bg-white, text-gray-500, border-gray-300). Name the role
instead, and both themes follow for free:



Role
Tokens




Backgrounds
surface, surface-raised (cards, menus, modals), surface-sunken, surface-muted, surface-hover, surface-inverse


Text
fg, fg-muted, fg-subtle, fg-faint (decorative only), fg-inverse


Borders
line (controls), line-subtle (dividers), line-strong


Brand
brand (fills), brand-hover, brand-fg (accent text), brand-accent (rings/borders), brand-tint, brand-tint-hover, on-brand


Semantic
danger, danger-fg, danger-tint, danger-border, on-danger, warning, warning-fg, warning-tint, success-fg, link, link-hover, info, info-hover, on-info


Chrome
bar, bar-fg, bar-fg-subtle (admin header, toasts — dark in both themes, so not surface-inverse), overlay



Text that sits on a coloured fill uses the fill’s own on-* token (bg-brand text-on-brand), not
text-fg-inverse — the latter flips with the theme, while lettering on a brand button stays white
in both.
Three rules that are easy to get wrong:

Elevation, not shadow. A raised surface must use bg-surface-raised; a shadow alone is
invisible in dark mode.
Never encode state in colour alone. A selected or active state also needs a shape, an icon or
an aria attribute — see #802 for
what happens otherwise.
fg-subtle and line only go on the page grounds (surface, surface-raised,
surface-sunken). On a filled panel — surface-muted or surface-hover — they drop under the
required ratio, so use fg-muted and line-strong there.

The location colours on the schedule are the one exception to the rule above: they stay palette
names, because a location’s colour is data. Put loc-<name> on the element and add the role class
for what you are drawing — loc-block, loc-block-dim, loc-badge, loc-tag, loc-swatch. Each
mixes the hue into the surface and foreground tokens in styles/tokens.css, so the same class works
in both themes — never write bg-${color}-500 again.
Token values live in styles/tokens.css and are the only place a colour is chosen.
tests/unit/theme-contrast.test.ts asserts the WCAG ratio of every pair in both themes, and
tests/unit/location-colors.test.ts does the same for all 22 location hues, so changing one tells
you what it broke. See ADR 0005.
Authorization
Every handler that modifies data must resolve the acting guest first — before validation — and
refuse to act as a protected guest without a verified session. This applies to REST routes, server
actions, and server components alike. Read-only surfaces are exempt.
Gating an action in the UI is never sufficient. Hiding an Edit button stops the honest path only;
the handler behind it is reachable directly. Where the UI restricts an operation to certain guests
(e.g. hosts), the handler must enforce the same rule independently.
Use cases apply the rule with actingGuest and actingAsNamedGuest from
server/kernel/acting

295.title: Documentation and the sites
295.text:
Documentation and the sites
Three sites, three audiences, three publishing rules:



Site
Built from
Published when




docs.schellingboard.org
docs/public/, at each tag
a release is tagged


developers.schellingboard.org
docs/dev/, on main
docs/dev/ changes on main


schellingboard.org
www/ + docs/screenshots/
www/ or the screenshots change



The split of audiences is the point: attendees and organizers read the first, contributors the
second, and nobody should land on the wrong one. Keeping the developer docs unversioned and the user
docs versioned follows from the same split — user docs must describe the release someone is running,
while developer docs must describe the branch they are working on.
The public docs site
Built with docmd from docs/public/, which holds one copy of the documentation
and no snapshots. Published versions are reconstructed from git: scripts/build-docs.sh walks the
release tags, checks each one out into a temporary worktree, and builds it as a version. The newest
is served at the site root, older ones under /<major.minor>/, all listed in the version dropdown.
So docs/public/ is the next release’s documentation. Edit it in the same commit as the change it
describes; it is published when that release is tagged.



Command
What it does




make docs
Live preview of docs/public


make docs-build
Build the published site into site/


make docs-validate
Check for broken internal links (runs in CI)



.github/workflows/docs.yml deploys on tag pushes and on pushes to release/* branches. Pushing to
main deliberately publishes nothing — until a release is tagged, make docs is the only place the
new documentation exists.
Two consequences worth knowing:

Releasing documentation is tagging the repository. There is no snapshot step, so nothing can
drift out of sync with the release it documents.
A release tag that predates the docs site publishes nothing. The build skips any tag without
docs/public/index.md, which is why v3.0.0 and v3.1.0 never appear on the site.

robots.txt, sitemap.xml and 404.html are generated by docmd from the config’s url; don’t
hand-write them.
Dating each page
Every page ends with “Last updated”, and the commits that touched it in a tooltip. docmd’s own git
plugin cannot produce that here: it delegates to its build engine, which runs git log in the
process working directory, so the worktrees the versions are built from are all “outside repository”
— the error is swallowed and the site publishes undated. scripts/docmd-git-history.js (loaded from
docmd.config.json as a local plugin) resolves the repository per page instead, which also means
each version is dated from its own ref rather than from main. Contributor avatars are deliberately
left off, so no reader’s browser is sent to Gravatar. build-docs.sh fails the build if any page
comes out undated.
Hosting setup for the docs site
Two things live outside the repository, so a fresh fork or a moved domain needs them set up again
before the first tag push can publish anything:

GitHub Pages: repository Settings → Pages → Source must be GitHub Actions.
actions/deploy-pages fails without it.
DNS: a CNAME record for docs.schellingboard.org pointing at schellingboard.github.io.
The domain itself comes from url in docmd.config.json — the build writes it to site/CNAME
from there.

Until both are in place and v3.2.0 is tagged, the
docs.schellingboard.org links in
README.md are dead; the
same pages are readable in docs/public/.
Correcting published documentation
To fix published docs without cutting a release, commit to the release branch of that version —
release/3.2 for the 3.2 docs. The build prefers that branch over the tag, so pushing it
republishes that version, and the deploy log names the ref each version came from
(Version 3.2 ← release/3.2).
Release branches don’t exist until something needs one. Create it from the release tag the first
time that minor release has to be corrected — a release that never needs a fix never gets a branch —
and merge it back into main so the fix reaches the next release too. The same branch carries the
commits of a patch release, so this is where a fix to an older version lives in general, not only a
documentation one; see Releasing a new version.
jj new v3.2.0
jj bookmark create release/3.2   # git: git switch -c release/3.2 v3.2.0
# fix, commit, push — the docs site redeploys

Because the branch tip wins over the tag, anything committed to it is published as that version’s
documentation the moment it is pushed, released or not. Land work that isn’t ready to be read on a
separate branch.
The developer docs site
The site you are reading. docmd.dev.config.mjs builds docs/dev/ into dev-site/ with its own
title, navigation and search index — a second docmd project in the same repository, sharing nothing
with the user site but the theme and the logo. ADR 0008 has
the reasoning, including why it isn’t a path under docs.schellingboard.org.



Command
What it does




make docs-dev
Live prev

308.title: Matrix chat integration — feasibility notes
308.text:
Matrix chat integration — feasibility notes
Status: exploratory, not decided. This is not an ADR — no decision has been made to build any of
this. It records what’s technically possible and what it costs, as input to that decision.
Goal
Let attendees jump from a profile/session in SchellingBoard to a chat with that person, without
requiring an existing Signal/Telegram/WhatsApp contact. Scope agreed so far:

One chat server per event, not shared across events, not federated with the public Matrix network.
Accounts auto-provisioned/synced from event participants.
1:1 chats and group chats (subset or all attendees).
Rooms with elevated permissions (e.g. an orga-only room).
A no-install web client is required; native/desktop clients are a bonus, not a replacement for it.
Chat is reached via a link to a separate URL (e.g. chat.sb.example.com) — it does not need
to be embedded in the SchellingBoard UI itself.
Voice/video: opt-in only, useful mainly for organizers, not part of the default feature.
Server-initiated notifications (e.g. “session moved to a different slot”) sent into Matrix,
targeted at attendees who RSVP’d.

Architecture
Server: Synapse (Matrix’s reference homeserver,
AGPL-3.0, open source), one container per event, alongside the existing app container. Isolation
from the public Matrix network: remove/firewall the federation listener (port 8448) and set
federation_domain_whitelist: []. No single config flag does this; it’s a combination, and Synapse
may still be able to originate some outbound federation traffic unless the listener is actually
blocked at the network level. (synapse#6401)
Provisioning: SchellingBoard’s server calls Synapse’s admin API (/_synapse/admin/v1/register,
HMAC-signed with a shared secret held only by the app container) to create/sync a Matrix account
when a guest is created. This is a server-to-server call; the shared secret is never exposed to a
browser. (Register API)
1:1 chat: a matrix.to link (https://matrix.to/#/@alice:sb.example.com)
on the attendee’s profile opens whatever Matrix client the visitor is signed into and starts/opens a
DM. No embedding needed to satisfy “jump from a profile to a chat.”
Group / orga rooms: created via the Client-Server API; membership managed by inviting/removing
the mapped Matrix IDs of the guests in the group. Elevated permissions (who can invite, redact,
change room settings) are native Matrix room
power levels — no extra tooling
required.
Server-initiated notifications: a bot/service account (created the same way as regular accounts)
posts into either a per-attendee DM or a per-session room, using the RSVP list SchellingBoard
already has server-side to decide who’s invited/ targeted. This slots in next to the existing
sessionHeadsUp email trigger in packages/contracts/src/guest.ts — same trigger point, an
additional send instead of/alongside the email.
Hosting under sb.example.com/messaging?
Not for the homeserver API. Synapse’s client/server API paths are hardcoded to start at
/_matrix and /_synapse/client from the root of whatever (sub)domain it’s served on; the official
reverse-proxy docs explicitly warn against inserting a path prefix in proxy_pass, since it breaks
URL canonicalisation (and, when federation is on, signature verification).
(reverse_proxy.html) A
subdirectory setup is DIY, undocumented, and risks subtly breaking media URLs and .well-known
discovery. The supported shape is a dedicated (sub)domain, e.g. chat.sb.example.com.
Clean-looking Matrix IDs are still possible via
well-known delegation:
sb.example.com can serve a static /.well-known/matrix/client (and /server, if federation were
ever wanted) JSON file pointing base_url at https://chat.sb.example.com, giving IDs like
@alice:sb.example.com while the actual homeserver runs on its own subdomain. This is a static file
the Next.js app (or the reverse proxy in front of it) can serve trivially, and doesn’t conflict with
anything else on the main domain.
The web client UI (Element Web or similar) is a static SPA and can be built for a subpath
(<base href> + matching web-server root), but the simplest and best-tested option is to serve it
from the same subdomain as the homeserver (chat.sb.example.com) rather than fight subpath
rewriting for no real benefit, given embedding isn’t required.
Embedding a chat UI directly in SchellingBoard (not required, but asked about)
Possible, but a real subproject, not a dependency you add:

matrix-js-sdk is headless (protocol/sync/E2EE
only) — a custom message list, composer, and room list would need to be built on top of it.
matrix-react-sdk is not an embeddable
component library — by its own docs it only works as part of Element Web’s own “skin” and isn’t
usable standalone.

Given chat can live at its own URL, this is not worth building unless attendees specifically ask for
it after using the link-out version.
Can this replace Signal/Telegram?
Mostly, with real gaps:



Area
Status




1:1/group text, files, reactions, E2EE
Works

323.title: Getting started
323.text:
Getting started
Technology stack

Server: Hono on Node; web app: React, Vite and TanStack Router
Language: TypeScript (strict mode)
Styling: Tailwind CSS
Database: SQLite (better-sqlite3) with Drizzle ORM
Testing: Vitest and Playwright
Package manager: Bun

Where things live:

Frontend: the single-page app in apps/web; see The web app
Database layer: db/ — schema.ts, container.ts, repositories in db/repositories/sqlite/
Server: use cases in server/modules/, the HTTP surface in server/http/
Utils: Shared utilities in utils/
Domain and contracts: workspace packages — packages/domain (vocabulary, constants, pure
rules) and packages/contracts (zod schemas); see ADR 0010
Migrations: Drizzle-managed SQL migrations in drizzle/

The architecture is written up separately in Architecture; the rules the
build enforces today are in Architecture rules.
Prerequisites

Bun (package manager and script runner)
Node.js 22 (or higher), installed and on your PATH. Although Bun runs the app, the tooling
shells out to a real node — bun x tsx for migrations/scripts, and Vitest’s test workers — so
node must be directly on your PATH. Check with node -v.

Setup

Clone the repo and install dependencies:
make install


(Optional) Create .env.dev.local to customize environment variables:
DATABASE_URL=file:./data.db
SITE_PASSWORD=your-password
AUTH_SECRET=<generated via openssl rand -base64 32>

See Environment variables below for all options. Note: AUTH_SECRET is
required only when SITE_PASSWORD is set or guests protect their name (it signs their session
cookies). Omitting this file uses sensible defaults.

(Optional) Seed the database with test data:
make dev-db-seed

This seeds the large profile: the hand-curated fixtures the E2E suite uses plus a few hundred
generated guests, proposals and sessions for realistic manual testing. Conference Gamma also gets
volunteer shifts (locations “Volunteers 1” and “Volunteers 2”, hosted by an organizer account),
attendee reports and 1-on-1 requests in every status, to try the admin statistics (move the dev
clock past Gamma to see it as an ended event). SEED_PROFILE=small make dev-db-seed seeds only
the curated fixtures (what the E2E suite always runs against).

Start the dev server:
make dev

Open http://localhost:3000 in your browser. That is the Vite dev server
for the SPA; it proxies the API to the server, which runs on the next port (3001). When it is
ready, it prints the test credentials: the site password, the seeded site admin and guests, and
Mailpit.


Development commands
Run make to see all available commands:
make          # List all commands
make dev      # Start dev server
make test     # Run tests
make lint     # Lint code
make format   # Format code

Before committing or pushing, run:
make precommit  # Format, lint, type check, and run all tests (incl. e2e)

Admin UI
A web admin UI is available at /admin for managing all core records: events (basic info, phases,
days), the global pools of users and locations, event↔guest and event↔location assignments,
moderation of proposals, sessions, and RSVPs, and site settings (title, description, and the
optional venue map). It is for site admins, who sign in at /admin; make dev-db-seed seeds one
(username site-admin, password seed-password), and make bootstrap-link prints a link that
makes another. It has its own layout, and the sign-in asks for SITE_PASSWORD first when one is
set.
Dev fake clock
Set SB_ENABLE_DEV_TOOLS=1 and visit any event page with ?dev=1 to get a toolbar for
time-traveling the app (real time / +1h / +1d / +7d / pick a date), so you can walk an event
through its proposal → voting → scheduling phases without editing dates in the database. It’s a
request-scoped cookie, inert unless the env var is set — safe to enable on a shared staging/demo
instance. See ADR 0004 for details.
Environment variables
See
Configuration
for the full list and descriptions.
For local development, DATABASE_URL is the only required variable — unlike Docker, no default is
provided (e.g. file:./data.db). AUTH_SECRET is additionally required when SITE_PASSWORD is set
or guests protect their name (it signs their session cookies); generate one with:
openssl rand -base64 32

A new variable a self-hoster can set has to reach three files: the reference table above,
docker-compose.yml (which forwards it into the container) and .env.docker.example (where they
fill it in). Nothing runs docker-compose.yml — it is the one file here whose only user is a
stranger — so tests/unit/docker-compose-env.test.ts compares the three and names whichever
variable fell out of step. If a variable deliberately doesn’t go through compose, record the reason
in that test instead.
Running multiple instances
Several clones or jj workspaces on one machine compete for the same ports. Give each clone
explicit, distinct ports in .env.dev.local and .env.test.local — see
Running multiple instances for which variable does what and a worked
two-clone example.
Database migrations
make

334.title: Creating and Reading GitHub Issues
334.text:
Creating and Reading GitHub Issues
This repo uses two conventions beyond GitHub’s built-in issue fields: an Issue Type (Task /
Bug / Feature) and a custom single-select Priority field (Urgent / High / Medium /
Low). Type and Priority carry that information instead of labels — the only labels in regular use
are the component: * ones below.
Component labels
Each issue should get one component: * label indicating the area it touches:



Label
Scope




component: proposals
Proposal creation/listing/editing


component: voting
Voting (table + Quick Voting)


component: scheduling
Sessions, session grid, scheduling phase


component: admin
/admin backend


component: attendees
Attendee list, profiles, RSVPs on profiles


component: 1-on-1s
1-on-1 meetings: booking, availability, column


component: auth
Login, passwords, protected accounts


component: infra & dev
CI, testing, tooling, perf, security, upgrades


component: notifications
Email and in-app notifications


component: ui/ux
Cross-cutting styling/layout/accessibility


component: other
Reviewed, no suitable component



gh issue create/edit can set labels directly (no GraphQL needed):
gh issue edit 123 -R schellingboard/schellingboard --add-label "component: scheduling"

Always pass -R schellingboard/schellingboard to gh issue/gh pr commands. Without it gh
infers the repo from git remotes and fails (not a git repository) when run from a workspace, a
jj-only checkout or a subdirectory.
Neither field is exposed by gh issue create/gh issue edit/gh issue view — both require the
GraphQL API (gh api graphql).
Reading an issue’s type and priority
gh issue view --json doesn’t expose either field. Use REST instead:
gh api repos/schellingboard/schellingboard/issues/123 --jq \
  '{type: .type.name, priority: (.issue_field_values[]? | select(.issue_field_name=="Priority") | .single_select_option.name)}'

IDs needed for mutations
Repo id, issue type ids, and the Priority field/option ids (stable, but re-fetch if unsure):
gh api graphql -f query='
{ repository(owner: "schellingboard", name: "schellingboard") {
    id
    issueTypes(first: 10) { nodes { id name } }
} }'

gh api graphql -f query='
{ repository(owner: "schellingboard", name: "schellingboard") {
    issueFields(first: 20) { nodes { ... on IssueFieldSingleSelect { id name options { id name } } } }
} }'

Known values as of 2026-09-29 (double-check if a query above disagrees):



Name
ID




Repo
R_kgDOUhaF9Q


Type: Task
IT_kwDOE75_iM40KuIP


Type: Bug
IT_kwDOE75_iM40KuIQ


Type: Feature
IT_kwDOE75_iM40KuIR


Priority field
IFSS_kgDOAs8wdA


Priority: Urgent
IFSSO_kgDOBOrxxw


Priority: High
IFSSO_kgDOBOrxyA


Priority: Medium
IFSSO_kgDOBOrxyQ


Priority: Low
IFSSO_kgDOBOrxyg



Creating an issue with type and priority set
gh api graphql -f query='
mutation($repo: ID!, $title: String!, $body: String!, $type: ID!, $prioField: ID!, $prioOpt: ID!) {
  createIssue(input: {
    repositoryId: $repo, title: $title, body: $body, issueTypeId: $type,
    issueFields: [{ fieldId: $prioField, singleSelectOptionId: $prioOpt }]
  }) { issue { number url } }
}' \
  -f repo=R_kgDOUhaF9Q \
  -f title="Issue title" \
  -f body="$(cat body.md)" \
  -f type=IT_kwDOE75_iM40KuIR \
  -f prioField=IFSS_kgDOAs8wdA \
  -f prioOpt=IFSSO_kgDOBOrxyg

Changing type/priority on an existing issue
Get the issue’s node id first (number is not a valid GraphQL id):
gh api graphql -f query='{ repository(owner: "schellingboard", name: "schellingboard") { issue(number: 123) { id } } }'

Then:
# Type
gh api graphql -f query='
mutation($issue: ID!, $type: ID!) {
  updateIssueIssueType(input: { issueId: $issue, issueTypeId: $type }) { issue { number } }
}' -f issue=<issue node id> -f type=<type id>

# Priority
gh api graphql -f query='
mutation($issue: ID!, $field: ID!, $opt: ID!) {
  setIssueFieldValue(input: { issueId: $issue, issueFields: [{ fieldId: $field, singleSelectOptionId: $opt }] }) { issue { number } }
}' -f issue=<issue node id> -f field=IFSS_kgDOAs8wdA -f opt=<priority option id>

Body format conventions
Match existing issues’ style:

Sections as needed, in this rough order: ## Overview / ## Current behavior /
## Proposed behavior (or ## Proposed change/## Proposed fix) / ## Why / ## Impact /
## Notes
Small bugs/tasks can just be a short paragraph — headers aren’t mandatory.
Reference file:line for code-specific bugs (e.g.
`server/modules/people/application/sign-in.ts:130`).
Keep it succinct; this is a scheduling app issue tracker, not a spec document.

342.title: Database Migrations
342.text:
Database Migrations
make dev-migrate-create (drizzle-kit generate) diffs db/schema.ts against the latest snapshot
in drizzle/meta/ and writes a new NNNN_*.sql file plus an updated
drizzle/meta/NNNN_snapshot.json and drizzle/meta/_journal.json.
make test applies every migration to each released version’s database as well as to an empty one,
so a migration that only fails against populated data fails there — see
Release-upgrade tests.
Resolving migration conflicts
When two branches each add a migration, drizzle/meta/_journal.json and the latest
drizzle/meta/NNNN_snapshot.json conflict — both branches claim the same index. Don’t hand-edit the
conflicted JSON; regenerate it instead:

Move your own new .sql migration file out of the way (e.g. to /tmp) so it doesn’t confuse
drizzle-kit. Note its name.

Restore drizzle/meta/ to the stable version (main), discarding your branch’s snapshot/journal
changes — db/schema.ts is unaffected, only the generated meta files reset:
# jj
jj restore --from main -- drizzle/meta

# Git
git checkout main -- drizzle/meta


Regenerate against the restored snapshot, in a real terminal (not piped/non-interactive — see
below):
make dev-migrate-create NAME=<original-migration-name>

--name gets you the right filename directly; without it you’d rename the auto-generated file
afterward (keep drizzle-kit’s index, drop the random suffix). If your change looks like a column
rename to drizzle-kit (e.g. drop one column, add another), it opens an interactive prompt asking
whether to treat it as a rename or a create+drop — it needs a real TTY, so this step can’t run
from a script or CI.

Diff the regenerated .sql file against the copy you moved aside in step 1. For a plain
mechanical schema change they’ll match — delete the moved-aside copy. But if your original
migration had hand-written SQL beyond what schema.ts alone implies (a data backfill, a value
transform, choosing “rename” over “create+drop”), the regenerated file won’t reproduce it —
drizzle-kit only knows what it can infer from the schema diff. In that case keep the
regenerated drizzle/meta/*_snapshot.json and journal entry (they carry the correct index),
but replace the regenerated file’s SQL body with your original hand-written SQL.

Run make dev-migrate-up to confirm the migration applies cleanly, then continue resolving the
rest of the conflict as usual.

345.title: Running Multiple Instances
345.text:
Running Multiple Instances
Several clones or jj workspaces of this project on one machine compete for the same ports. The
recommended pattern is to give each clone explicit, distinct ports in its two local env files,
rather than leaning on defaults or automatic port selection — then nothing depends on which instance
you happened to start first. Neither file is committed:



File
Read by
Sets




.env.dev.local
make dev, make mailpit
dev server port, mailpit’s host ports, email


.env.test.local
make test, make test-e2e
email (opt-in, see Running tests)



Start mailpit with make mailpit rather than a bare docker compose up mailpit: mailpit is defined
in docker-compose.dev.yml (not in the docker-compose.yml self-hosters copy), and on its own
compose reads only a file literally named .env, so the make target passes both -f and
--env-file .env.dev.local. That keeps each clone’s ports in one place.
Example: two clones side by side
Clone A in ~/src/sb-a keeps the defaults:
# .env.dev.local
DATABASE_URL=file:./data.db
AUTH_SECRET=<openssl rand -base64 32>
PORT=3000
SITE_URL=http://localhost:3000
COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=sb-a
MAILPIT_SMTP_PORT=1025
MAILPIT_UI_PORT=8025
SMTP_FROM=dev@example.test
SMTP_URL=smtp://localhost:1025

# .env.test.local
SMTP_URL=smtp://localhost:1025
MAILPIT_API_URL=http://localhost:8025
SMTP_FROM='Test <mailer-test@test.example>'

Clone B in ~/src/sb-b shifts every port by one:
# .env.dev.local
DATABASE_URL=file:./data.db
AUTH_SECRET=<openssl rand -base64 32>
PORT=3001
SITE_URL=http://localhost:3001
COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=sb-b
MAILPIT_SMTP_PORT=1026
MAILPIT_UI_PORT=8026
SMTP_FROM=dev@example.test
SMTP_URL=smtp://localhost:1026

# .env.test.local
SMTP_URL=smtp://localhost:1026
MAILPIT_API_URL=http://localhost:8026
SMTP_FROM='Test <mailer-test@test.example>'

Each clone can now run make mailpit, make dev, make test, and make test-e2e at the same time
as the other. Not every line is always needed: COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME, MAILPIT_SMTP_PORT, and
MAILPIT_UI_PORT are consumed by docker compose rather than the app, and the SMTP_*/SITE_URL
lines only matter if you want the dev server itself to send email — PORT alone is enough
otherwise.
What each variable is for
Mailpit publishes two host ports, and the two app-side variables that point at them are unrelated to
each other — each tracks a different one:



Compose variable
Default
Mailpit port for
App-side variable to match




MAILPIT_SMTP_PORT
1025
receiving mail over SMTP
SMTP_URL


MAILPIT_UI_PORT
8025
the web UI and its REST API
MAILPIT_API_URL




SMTP_URL (utils/mailer.ts) is how schellingboard sends mail: an ordinary SMTP connection
string, with mailpit merely one possible server behind it.
MAILPIT_API_URL (tests/helpers/mailpit.ts) is how the test suite reads mail back out of
mailpit to assert on it. It is test-only and mailpit-specific; the app itself never reads it.

PORT is the port make dev serves the SPA on; the server runs on the next one. Set it for a
second instance, or the second make dev fails on the taken port. SITE_URL must agree with
PORT, since it’s the base URL emails use to link back to the site; a stale value sends readers to
the other instance.
COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME only matters when two clones share a directory name — compose derives the
project from the directory, so ~/a/sb and ~/b/sb would otherwise fight over a single mailpit
container. Setting it is cheap insurance. Note that mailpit lives in its own compose file, so a bare
docker compose down won’t stop it; use the same two flags make mailpit passes —
docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml --env-file .env.dev.local down — since without the env
file compose looks for the container under the directory-derived project name instead. (Or just
Ctrl-C the foreground make mailpit.)
Some things need no attention: DATABASE_URL and SB_UPLOADS_DIR are relative paths, so each clone
already gets its own database and uploads. E2E runs pick a free port per run and override SITE_URL
to match (playwright.config.ts), so don’t set SITE_URL in .env.test.local expecting it to
apply — only SMTP_URL and MAILPIT_API_URL matter there. make test binds no port at all.

349.title: Releasing a New Version
349.text:
Releasing a New Version
Pushing the tag is the whole release: it triggers
.github/workflows/release.yml,
which builds the image, runs the E2E suite against it, publishes it to Docker Hub and opens the
GitHub release — and
docs.yml,
which rebuilds the docs site and serves docs/public/ as of that tag at its root. Docs are
versioned per minor release, so v3.2.1 republishes the 3.2 documentation.

Finalize the changelog — in CHANGELOG.md, rename ## [Unreleased] to
## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD (no v prefix in the header), and replace the [Unreleased] compare
link at the bottom of the file with the new version’s, pointing from the previous release’s
endpoint to the new tag (vX.Y.Z). Do not add a fresh ## [Unreleased] section here — the
released tag should carry no empty section, since that is what the documentation site publishes.
Step 4 reopens it afterwards.
Release the in-app notes in the same commit — in packages/domain/src/release-notes.ts, the
first entry of releaseNotes is the one being prepared: replace its version: "Unreleased" with
this version and add the date. Nothing else moves. make test fails until the newest release
the changelog names has an entry.
Re-read those highlights against the finalized changelog first. They were written one at a
time, before it was known what else the release would hold, so they are a draft, not a record:
check that they are still the 3-5 changes an attendee or organizer would call this release’s
highlights, and rewrite or replace any that are not.
Record the release’s database in the same commit, so future releases are tested against an
upgrade from it:
make dump-release-db VERSION=vX.Y.Z

It writes no dump when the release ships no migration, only the
tests/fixtures/upgrade/releases.json entry pointing at the dump that already covers the
upgrade. make test fails until the version the changelog now names appears there, so the
fixture cannot be forgotten — and being in the release commit, it is inside the tag, where a
patch release branched off that tag needs it. See
Release-upgrade tests.
Commit and merge this like any other change.

Tag the resulting commit on main and push the tag — the point of no return, since it
publishes the documentation:
jj git fetch
jj tag set v3.0.0 -r main@origin
jj git push --tag v3.0.0
# git: git fetch origin main
#      git tag v3.0.0 origin/main
#      git push origin v3.0.0

Optionally run make test-e2e-docker on the release commit first. The release workflow runs it
too, and refuses to publish anything if it fails — running it locally only buys you the chance to
fix a failure before the tag is public.

Watch the release workflow. It takes around fifteen minutes, most of it the E2E suite against
the image.

Reopen the changelog — in a follow-up commit on main, add an empty ## [Unreleased]
section above ## [X.Y.Z] and an [Unreleased] compare link from vX.Y.Z to HEAD. Reopen
the in-app notes too — in packages/domain/src/release-notes.ts, add a new first entry with
version: "Unreleased" and no date, above the one just released.


What the release workflow does
Triggered by a v*.*.* tag, in one job, so nothing is published until everything before it has
passed:

Builds the image through scripts/docker-build.sh — the same script make docker-build runs
— with APP_VERSION taken from the tag rather than from scripts/app-version.js, which asks jj
or git describe and can’t be trusted on a CI checkout.
Runs the E2E suite against that image (make test-e2e-docker, with IMAGE naming the image
just built, so it is not rebuilt). This is the only tier that runs the artifact we ship, and the
last chance to catch a fault that exists only in it — a file the Dockerfile didn’t copy, a path
that resolves differently under /data, a date rendered in the server’s timezone rather than the
event’s. See Testing the Docker image. The report and the
traces of failed attempts are uploaded as an artifact.
Pushes four tags to schellingboard/schellingboard: the full version, major.minor, major,
and latest. scripts/release-tags.ts decides the last one from the repository’s tags —
:latest has to keep meaning the newest published release, so a patch cut from an older line
(v3.3.2 released after v3.4.0) publishes its own three tags and leaves :latest alone.
Creates the GitHub release, last, so a release exists only once its images do. It is marked as
GitHub’s “latest” on the same condition as the :latest tag.

Images are linux/amd64 only, which is what has always been published.
Repository configuration
The workflow needs two repository secrets:



Secret
Value




DOCKERHUB_USERNAME
The Docker Hub account that can push to schellingboard/schellingboard.


DOCKERHUB_TOKEN
A Docker Hub access token for that account with Read & Write scope — not the account password.



Nothing else: the GitHub release is created with the automatic GITHUB_TOKEN, which the workflow
grants contents: write.
If it fails
Nothing has been published unless the run reached the “Publis

356.title: The server and the API
356.text:
The server and the API
server/ holds the use cases and the /api/v1 HTTP API in front of them. The API and the jobs loop
call the same use cases, so a rule is written once. ADR 0012 has the
decisions; this page is how the code is laid out and how to add to it. The user-facing description
of the API is HTTP API.
Layout
server/
  kernel/              Result and error kinds, Actor and resolveActor (`actorOf` binds it to the session rows), actingGuest, the unit of work
  http/                the Hono app (app.ts), middleware, problem details, OpenAPI document and its reference page (docs.ts)
  feed/                the snapshot and the SSE change feed (routes.ts), the hub of open connections, projection of a change to a viewer
  composition.ts       builds each module's use cases from the repositories and adapters
  modules/<module>/
    module.ts          the only file anything outside the module imports
    ports.ts           its dependencies: a Pick of the repository container, plus adapters
    application/       use cases and queries, gathered in use-cases.ts
    http/              route declarations and handlers

The modules are sessions (sessions, RSVPs, room unavailability, attendee counts), proposals
(proposals and votes), comments, meetings, people (profiles and the admin guest list),
notifications, events (events and days), venue (locations), settings (site settings) and
updates (the daily GitHub look-up of the latest release, shown to the admin) and stats (the
read-only admin statistics, ADR 0019: one StatsRepository.getEventFacts
read, tables computed in the use case, CSV and ZIP from the routes).
server/main.ts runs the Hono app in server/http/web.ts on @hono/node-server, in its own Node
process, and starts the mailer and the jobs loop. scripts/build-server.ts bundles it with esbuild
into dist/server/main.mjs. The app gates /api/v1 (site password; a guest cookie for
/api/v1/admin/, whose use cases check the site-admin role), serves /media, the public files, the
manifest and the SPA, and adds the security headers. Repositories stay in db/.
db/container.ts opens the database in WAL mode with two connections. Repository methods named
find… (but not findOrCreate…), list…, search…, count… or get… run on a read-only
connection, which sees only committed rows. Every other method takes the in-process write lock and
runs on the write connection, so name a method that writes accordingly
(ADR 0013).
A use case writes in deps.uow.run(async (tx) => …) (server/kernel/unit-of-work.ts): one
transaction, which a throw or a failure Result rolls back. Inside it, read and write through tx,
never through deps.repos: their writes wait for the lock tx holds, and their reads do not see
its rows. tx.record(change) logs a change with the state, addressed to the audience audienceOf
(packages/domain/src/change.ts) gives (add a case for each new type; none is for changes logged
only for reactions, which no feed viewer sees) and marked with the request’s Idempotency-Key, if
any; after commit, each change goes to the subscribeToChanges subscribers in seq order, the jobs
loop among them. Keep I/O to other systems, such as mail, out of the callback. uow.read runs
several reads on one consistent view.
Reading for pages
Site pages do not call the repositories. pageReads() in composition.ts gives plain reads (no
actor: the pages sit behind the site password only). Each is a function in a module’s
application/page-reads.ts taking a Pick of the repositories. make arch enforces it, with the
auth flows allow-listed.
Choosing a name
PUT /api/v1/me/identity makes the browser act as an open guest name; GET answers who the browser
acts as now (null for a protected name not yet logged in, the SPA’s viewer); PUT sets the guest
cookie, which the route adapter builds from the use case’s Identity
(people/application/identity.ts). A protected name answers 403 guest.protected: the SPA sends
the user to the sign-in. POST /auth/site takes the shared site password (open to visitors without
the cookie; site.passwordWrong, and auth.tooManyAttempts per address) and sets the site cookie;
DELETE /auth/site clears it and ends the login session (not rate limited).
Signing in
POST /api/v1/auth/login-code emails a code, POST /auth/login takes the password or that code and
sets a verified session cookie, POST /auth/sign-out ends it (people/application/sign-in.ts).
/auth/* has its own per-address rate limit on top of the per-guest password limit and the daily
email cap, and a limit answers 429 (kind limited). Problem codes: auth.credentialWrong (wrong,
spent or expired password or code, indistinguishable on purpose), auth.tooManyAttempts,
auth.codeRecentlySent, auth.codeSpent, auth.tooManyEmails, auth.mailUnavailable,
auth.mailFailed. A limited refusal carries Retry-After. The web gate refuses a cross-site
/api/v1/auth/* request like the admin API’s (403 request.crossSite). The per-address limit
applies only with SB_TRUSTED_PROXIES set; its burst is

366.title: Statistics in the admin: later
366.text:
Statistics in the admin: later
The statistics are decided in ADR 0019 and the figures are listed in
Statistics: figures. Issue #389 is the brainstorm. This note keeps what is not
built.
Later: what to collect for better statistics
Rough; each item needs its own design and an entry in the data collection statement (#801).

Coarse timestamps on votes and RSVPs (to the hour): voting and RSVP timelines, “how late do
people RSVP”. Deleted with the vote or RSVP.
Aggregate counters without people: RSVP cancellations per session, notification clicks per
type, feature use per day (schedule, map, search). No ids, no addresses, no third-party analytics.
Daily snapshots: the jobs loop writes a few event-wide counts per day to a table, since the
change log is pruned. Gives history without per-person rows.
Attendance confirmation: an attendee taps “I was there” (opt-in). Better than host counts and
RSVPs. Stored as an RSVP flag, so it goes with the RSVP.
Anonymous ratings after a session (#389, #1053): store the rating without a guest id; prevent
a second rating with a separate “rated” row per (guest, session), deleted after the event.
Device class (phone, desktop) per login session, not the user agent.
Rules for all of it: data minimisation (collect what a figure needs, coarsen times), no
per-person data that outlives the person’s account, k ≥ 3 for anything shown, documented purpose
and retention, aggregates only for anything kept after the event.

369.text:
Statistics in the admin: figures
The design of the admin’s “Statistics” area (/admin/statistics/{event}). The decisions (privacy
rules, filter, table contract, CSV, chart library) are in ADR 0019; this
note lists the data and the figures.
Goal
An organizer, during and after an event, answers: did the process work (proposals → votes → sessions
→ attendance), did the venue work (rooms, gaps, peak times), and which features people used
(1-on-1s, profiles, comments, notifications). Every figure is a table that downloads as CSV, and
most have a chart. The same page serves a past event after an upgrade.

Past events. An organizer upgrades an old database (e.g. 3.8.1) and opens the page. A figure
whose data an older release did not collect (attendee counts before 3.6.0, 1-on-1s before they
existed) says “No data”, never 0. The release-upgrade fixtures check that the page works on every
migrated release.
Figures
Each section is a set of figures. A figure is: a table (sortable, CSV) and, where it helps, a chart.
The SPA shows each as a card with an explanation (features/admin/stats-figures.tsx, the
catalogue); a big table’s charts get cards of their own there. Bold marks the figures we think
matter most.
1. Overview

Headline numbers: members, active members (voted, RSVPed, proposed, hosted, commented or
offered 1-on-1 times), voters, RSVPers, proposals, sessions, hosts, sessions with an attendee
report.
Participation funnel (chart: horizontal bars): members → active → voted → RSVPed → hosted.
Who did what (aggregate overlap): how many members voted only, RSVPed only, both, neither;
mean RSVPs of voters vs non-voters. This answers “do voters engage more” without a joinable table.

2. Proposals and voting

Proposal funnel table, one row per proposal: title, hosts, created, duration, cohost wanted,
interested / maybe / skip, voters, interest share s, rank, became a session, the session’s
RSVPs, reported attendees, comments. This is the “votes → RSVPs → attendance” line asked for.
Chart: ranked bars of interest, coloured by “became a session”.
Popular but never scheduled: the top-quartile proposals without a session. Short list, high
value.
Late proposals get fewer votes? Scatter: created time vs voters, ρ. Tells the organizer
whether the proposal phase or the voting phase was too short.
Proposals over time: proposals created per day per day (line; no phase bands).
Votes per voter (per-person, pseudonymous): total, interested, maybe, skip, share of proposals
covered. Chart: histogram of totals. Also: share of voters who voted on every proposal.
Choice mix: interested / maybe / skip overall, and a histogram of each voter’s interested
share (“picky vs generous” voters).
Hosts and proposals: proposals per host (histogram), co-hosted proposals, cohost wanted vs
cohost found.
Conversion: proposals → sessions, by interest quartile. A proposal “became a session” if it
has any session, even one the filter removes; its RSVPs and report come from a kept session only.

3. Sessions

Session table, one row per session: title, origin, day, start, end, duration, locations,
hosts, capacity, RSVPs, fill (RSVPs / capacity), reported attendees, attendees per RSVP, closed,
parallel sessions (others overlapping it), proposal votes, comments.
Sessions by popularity: ranked bars of RSVPs, with the capacity as a tick and reported
attendees as a second mark.
Origins: count and median RSVPs per origin (proposal / spontaneous / organizer).
Hosts: sessions hosted, unique hosts, share of members who hosted, sessions per host
(histogram), sessions with more than one host.
Attendance reports — did hosts report? Ended sessions with hosts, sessions reported, share;
the same by origin and by day; hosts asked vs hosts who reported at least once; share reported

be trusted.
Attendance: attendees vs RSVPs scatter with ρ; attendees per RSVP distribution (the “no-show”
